newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl's coalition meets to discuss budget crisis.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's coalition meets to discuss budget crisis.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition on Wednesday will begin hammering out the details of a budget package aimed at easing strains in the government and rescuing Bonn's bid to join Europe's single currency.

Highlighting the urgency of the situation, Finance Minister Theo Waigel has accelerated plans to sell off state holdings and will skip the June 20-22 summit of the Group of Seven (G7) wealthy industrial nations to put his own house in order.

Kohl's beleaguered coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU), Christian Social Union (CSU) and Free Democrats (FDP) has been closer to collapse than ever before in its 14 year history as the parties clash over how to mend gaping holes in the budget.
"The coalition is not out of the woods yet because we have not resolved the practical problems," said Otto Lambsdorf, a former FDP economics minister.

The hot phase of budget deliberations is July 10-11, when coalition party leaders will work out the final draft and present it to their parliamentary groups and approve it in cabinet. Final passage in parliament is expected in November.
The coalition is still split over how to finance holes torn in the budget by a sharp fall in tax revenues and high spending resulting from record unemployment levels.

The tax-cutting FDP has ruled out any tax increases to fill the budget and instead said it would present proposals to step up privatisations that could bring the federal government some 40 billion marks ($23 billion) in revenue over the next two years.
"With a combination of privatisation and spending cuts we want to tackle 20 billion marks for 1997 and 30 billion marks for 1998," said FDP chairman Wolfgang Gerhard.
Original plans for the 1998 federal budget show an increase in spending of around seven billion marks to 447 billion marks and an estimated budget deficit of 58 billion marks.

The 1997 budget deficit was forecast at 53.3 billion marks, but Waigel is widely expected to be preparing a supplementary budget that could include a higher deficit if the shortfalls cannot be offset by privatisation revenue and spending cuts.
After Wednesday's coalition meeting, Waigel will begin making the rounds to the 15 government ministries seeking further savings of some five billion marks next year, coalition sources said.
But resistance to new budget cuts is already mounting.
Rainer Eppelmann, head of the labour wing of Kohl's CDU, said further cuts in social welfare budgets was unimaginable.
"Even Chancellor Kohl is of the opinion that there is nothing more to be taken out of this budget," Eppelmann said.

To head off a palace revolt over budget cuts, Bonn appears to agree it must concentrate on selling off government holdings such as its stakes in phone giant Deutsche Telekom and Deutsche Postbank, which could raise 10 billion marks this year.
And coalition sources say that the divisive issue of tax cuts -- most likely value added taxes or petrol taxes -- cannot be entirely ruled out, despite staunch FDP resistance.

Much to the displeasure of industry, the coalition is also considering financing a planned reduction in the solidarity tax -- a surcharge on income tax bills to finance German unification -- by cutting corporate tax breaks.

The hectic search for cash to plug the budget deficit has put the government on a collision course with the Bundesbank and has Waigel rummaging in every corner to find unneeded state assets that could be sold to the public.

After Bonn's failed bid to force the Bundesbank to revalue its gold and currency reserves to raise funds to pay off state debt, Bonn confirmed it was considering selling crude oil reserves that were stock-piled after the 1970s Arab oil embargo to protect against shortages and price shocks.

Bonn has a list of some 400 holdings it wants to sell before autumn 1998 including real estate companies, airports, coal mines and motorway service station chain Tank und Rast AG - estimated to be worth some 700 million marks.
The cabinet is expected to set up a working group in the next few weeks that will begin making concrete plans to carry out the privatisation programme.
-- william.boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150) ($ = 1.731 German Marks)
